newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANBERRA WATCH-Government's senate strength still undiminished.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH-Government's senate strength still undiminished.

text.p: Prime Minister John Howard's promise to neutralise senator Mal Colston's support for the government makes no practical difference to Senate votes.
As Canberra Watch pointed out seven weeks ago, the independent senator must depart and be replaced by a Labor member to affect voting results.
The only advance between then and now is that the departure of Colston, who is accused of corruption, may have become closer.
It makes no difference if a government senator abstains from a vote to neutralise Colston's support, as Howard promised today.

Unless and until Colston does depart, the government can still win votes and therefore get any crucial legislation through the Senate providing the Labor rebel does not return to voting with his former colleagues, which is highly unlikely.
The reason for this is that a motion passes the Senate if more senators vote for it than against it. That means that if the vote is tied, the motion fails.
This may seem like the bleeding obvious, but it explains why it does not matter whether Colston's vote for the government is counted or not.
There are 76 senators -- 37 Liberal-National, 28 Labor, seven Democrat, two Greens and independents Brian Harradine and Colston.
If 76 senators vote, a motion will need 39 votes to pass, because 38-all is not enough.

For the government, that 39 has to be assembled from their own 37 plus the two independents, since the Green Laborcrats (to borrow the term of analyst Malcolm Mackerras) oppose almost everything controversial.
That's why Colston's defection was crucial last year.
But his absence -- or the absence of another senator in his place -- produces the same result.
If 75 senators vote, then a motion needs 38 votes (more than half) to pass.
The government has 38 votes if it can get Harradine alone. If Colston also backs a government motion and a government senator abstains, then the ruling coalition still has 38 votes.
So the government's position is undiminished by today's announcement.

The focus remains on the crucial question of the Queensland senator leaving parliament, and the driving issue here is the constitution's exclusion from parliament of anyone convicted of a serious offence.
If he leaves, the constitution would require the Queensland government to replace him with a Labor senator, restoring the total number of senators to 76 and the vote-winning target to 39.
Last week, some of the many allegations against Colston -- all of which he denies -- were referred to the police.
So we now wait to see whether the police prosecute and, if they do, whether he is convicted.
For Canberra Watchers concerned about the government legislative programme, that remains the crucial issue.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
